citeinfo.title: High-resolution maps of historical and 21st century soil temperature and moisture data using multivariate matching algorithms for drylands of western U.S. and Canada

descript.abstract: These data were compiled as a supplement to a previously published journal article (Bradford et al., 2019), that employed a ecosystem water balance model to characterize current and future patterns in soil temperature and moisture conditions in dryland areas of western North America. Also, these data are associated with a published USGS data release (Bradford and Schlaepfer, 2019). The objectives of our study were to (1) characterize current and future patterns in soil temperature and moisture conditions in dryland areas of western North America, (2) evaluate the impact of these changes on estimation of resilience and resistance among a representative set of climate scenarios. These data represent geographic patterns in simulated soil temperature and soil moisture conditions and underlying variables based on SOILWAT2 simulations under climate conditions representing historical (current) time period (1980-2010) and two future projected time periods (2020-2050, d40yrs) and (2070-2100, d90yrs) for two representative concentration pathways (RCP4.5, RCP8.5) as medians across simulation runs based on output from each of the available downscaled global circulation models that participated in CMIP5 (RCP4.5, 37 GCMs; RCP8.5, 35 GCMs; Maurer et al. 2007). Additional information about the SOILWAT2 simulation experiments can be found in Bradford et al. 2019. These data were created in 2018, 2019, and 2021 for the area of the sagebrush region in the western North America. These data were created by a collaborative research project between the U.S. Geological Survey, Marshall University and Yale University. These data can be used with the high-resolution matching as defined by Renne et al. (in prep.), and within the scope of Bradford et al. 2019. These data may also be used to evaluate the potential impact of changing climate conditions on geographic patterns in simulated soil temperature and soil moisture conditions.
descript.purpose: The purpose of these data is to describe geographic patterns in simulated soil moisture and soil temperature conditions under historical and projected future climate conditions at a 30-arcsec spatial resolution. These data can be used to to evaluate soil moisture and soil temperature conditions (Bradford et al. 2019) and/or high resolution matching of those soil moisture and soil temperature conditions as implemented by Renne et al. (in prep.) and within the scope defined by the study. These data were created to delineate geographic patterns in simulated soil temperature and soil moisture conditions and underlying variables based on SOILWAT2 simulations under various climate conditions (Bradford et al., 2019) and high resolution matching as defined by Renne et al. (in prep.). These data may also be used to evaluate the potential impact of changing climate conditions on geographic patterns in simulated soil temperature and soil moisture conditions.
descript.supplinf: These data are based on an ecosystem water balance model, parameterized with the spatially-explicit input data described above. Thus, geographic patterns in these data are inherently limited to the types of variation in the climate and soil data used as inputs. Users are encouraged to examine the details of the accuracy before use of any of these data. We cannot guarantee accuracy of the data, and use is at the risk of the user. Data users should read the entire metadata record and acquire manuscripts identified as ‘Cross Reference' to have a complete understanding of how these data were created and used. The data are specific to the uses identified above, to evaluate the high resolution matching of ecological drought metrics (Renne et al. 202X), and/or the robust soil drought conditions as defined by Bradford et al. 2019, within a scope as defined by this study, and any other use of these data would be inappropriate. See 'Distribution liability' statements for more information.

procstep.procdesc:
INPUT DATA:: We downloaded output from 37 GCMs (ACCESS1-0, ACCESS1-3, bcc-csm1-1, bcc-csm1-1-m, BNU-ESM, CanESM2, CCSM4, CESM1-BGC, CESM1-CAM5, CMCC-CM, CNRM-CM5, CSIRO-Mk3-6-0, EC-EARTH, FGOALS-g2, FGOALS-s2, FIO-ESM, GFDL-CM3, GFDL-ESM2G, GFDL-ESM2M, GISS-E2-H-CC, GISS-E2-R, GISS-E2-R-CC, HadGEM2-AO, HadGEM2-CC, HadGEM2-ES, inmcm4, IPSL-CM5A-LR, IPSL-CM5A-MR, IPSL-CM5B-LR, MIROC-ESM, MIROC-ESM-CHEM, MIROC5, MPI-ESM-LR, MPI-ESM-MR, MRI-CGCM3, NorESM1-M, NorESM1-ME) downscaled for North America from the “Downscaled CMIP3 and CMIP5 Climate and Hydrology Projects” archive (http://gdo-dcp. ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections; Maurer et al. 2007). GeoTIFFs for each variable were created using the R package “raster” (Hijmans 2021) and the GDAL library in 2021. A comprehensive description of the development of all GeoTIFF variables is included in Bradford et al. 2019 in the methods section.
A simulation experiment modeled ecosystem water balance on a grid with 10 km resolution across the U.S. and Canada with 58,694 grid cells for which soil properties (sand %, clay %, volume of gravel, and bulk density) for 12 soil layers with a maximal depth of 150 cm were extracted from NRCS STATSGO (1 km2 grids; https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/wps/portal/nrcs/detail/soils/survey/geo/?cid=nrcseprd1464625) and ISRIC-WISE v1.2 (5-arcmin; https://data.isric.org/geonetwork/srv/eng/catalog.search#/metadata/82f3d6b0-a045-4fe2-b960-6d05bc1f37c0) for Canada (Bradford et al. 2019). Daily meteorological data were extracted from near-surface gridded observed meteorological data (Livneh et al. 2013) for the U.S. and from historical (1980–2010) climate grids for Canada (McKenney et al. 2011). For two future periods, 2020–2050 and 2069–2099, monthly time-series were extracted from climate projections (1/8 degree in the United States, 1⁄2 degree in Canada) from all available GCMs for two representative concentration pathways (RCP 4.5—37 GCMs; RCP 8.5—35 GCMs) from the "Downscaled CMIP3 and CMIP5 Climate and Hydrology Projections" BCSD-monthly archive (Maurer et al. 2007) at http://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downs caled_cmip_projections/.

DATA PROCESSING:: The simulation experiment by Bradford et al. (2019) simulated ecosystem water balance on a grid with 10 km resolution across the U.S. and Canada and quantified drought metrics in dryland areas where the ratio of mean annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration was < 0.6. Soil moisture dynamics were simulated with the SOILWAT2 ecosystem water balance model (Schlaepfer et al. 2021) under climate conditions representing historical ("current") time period (1980-2010) and two future projected time periods (2020-2050) and (2070-2100) for two representative concentration pathways (RCP4.5, RCP8.5) as medians across simulation runs based on output from each of the available downscaled global circulation models that participated in CMIP5 (RCP4.5, 37 GCMs; RCP8.5, 35 GCMs; Maurer et al. 2007).

FINAL OUTPUT(S): Final outputs were processed in 2021 using multivariate matching algorithm (Renne et al., in prep.) which transfers simulated soil moisture conditions (Bradford et al. 2019) from an original 10-km resolution to a 30-arcsec spatial resolution.

Data Quality Assessment and Quality Control (QAQC): Geographic patterns and summary statistics for these data were visually inspected for consistency and reasonableness during analysis in 2019, 2020 and 2021. We created and examined maps of values to evaluate the geographic patterns, and generated boxplots of distributions to identify potential outlier values. These data were also summarized and evaluated as part of Bradford et al. 2019.
